description: Normative global 1.5°C aligned pathway that achieves net zero emissions by 2050.
pathwayDescription: The IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) Scenario is a normative 1.5 aligned pathway, outlining how the global energy sector can reach net zero CO2 emissions by 2050. It assumes that advanced economies achieve net zero earlier (by mid 2040s), with emerging markets following by 2050. As a normative scenario, the NZE provides a detailed description of one pathway to reach a targeted future state, but it does not attempt to predict which policies or outcomes are most probable. The NZE pathway corresponds to a 50% probability of 1.5°C of warming by 2100. This is a more ambitious outcome than the IEA’s Announced Pledges Scenario (APS), which projects 1.7°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability), indicating a significant gap remains between announced governmental pledges and the trajectory described by the NZE pathway.

coreDrivers.policies: The NZE pathway expands on currently stated policies and NDC targets. Carbon prices are introduced in all regions and cover most sectors, rising to USD 250/t CO2 by 2050 in advanced economies and USD 200/t CO2 in emerging markets, phase-out dates are explicit and binding as unabated coal-fired generation falls 85% by 2035 and is completely phased out by 2040.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: This pathway is defined by reaching net zero energy-related CO2 emissions by 2050. The target is also expressed as a temperature outcome, consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 C with limited overshoot at a 50% probability. Advanced economies are constrained to reach net zero by mid 2040s with emerging market and developing economies following by 2050.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Unit technology costs are endogenous and deployment-linked: future cost evolution is tied to deployment levels, following a non-linear learning curve.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-carbon investment rises sharply as a share of total energy investment. Oil and gas supply investment falls to USD 250 billion in 2035, around 70% below today, while clean energy spending grows in all sectors with the largest increases in grids and storage, buildings and transport.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population follows the UN medium variant, reaching 9.68 billion in 2050, and GDP grows from USD 175,981 billion to USD 357,510 billion (2023, PPP).
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: An international co-operation and burden-sharing assumption shapes the regional distribution of the pathway: achieving net zero energy sector CO2 by 2050 "depends on fair and effective global co-operation, with advanced economies taking the lead and reaching net zero emissions earlier in the NZE Scenario than emerging market and developing economies". Advanced economies reach -583 Mt CO2 in 2050 while the world total is exactly zero.

dependencies.dependency_description: The pathway outcome is not feasible without policy that goes well beyond anything pledged. Carbon prices are introduced in all regions covering most sectors, unabated coal generation is phased out completely by 2040, and universal energy access is delivered by 2030. Failure to resolve constraints would jeopardize the 2050 target.

Grid line length has to grow about 20% by 2030, and delivery at that rate is not feasible under permitting and planning processes that currently take over a decade per grid project. The publication states that significant grid enhancements are required and that expansion calls for regulatory and planning change.

The pathway requires both rapid scale-up of clean energy finance and contraction of fossil finance. Oil and gas supply investment falls to USD 250 billion by 2035, around 70% below today, so many new projects face major commercial risks and some may fail to recover their upfront costs. On the other side, clean energy spending has to grow in every sector with the largest increases in grids and storage, buildings and transport, much of it in economies where capital costs are highest.

The physical exposure is clear (grid length, nuclear/hydro capacity rising) but the evidence base is a passing remark, and the pathway contains no acceptance analysis, no polling and no mitigation proposal.

The pathway requires the electricity share of final consumption to reach 54.5% by 2050, from 20.4% in 2023, at the same time as total final consumption falls from 444.7 to 344.1 EJ - so households and firms must both electrify and consume less.

The pathways infrastructure must outpace anything built historically. Grid line length has to grow about 20% by 2030 and storage capacity to 5 512 GW by 2050, and with unabated coal fully phased out by 2040 the system loses the firm capacity that currently provides adequacy and storage, interconnection and flexibility have to substitute for it rather than supplement it. Hydrogen adds a second handling, storage and transport infrastructure requirement.

The pathway is not feasible on the current technology set. Captured CO2 reaches 5 924 Mt by 2050 and DAC 780 Mt, emissions hydrogen production 38.1 EJ, BECCS 731 TWh, and hydrogen and ammonia 443 GW of power capacity, all from bases at or near zero today. Because costs are endogenous and deployment-linked, the cost assumptions and the deployment assumptions are mutually dependent, so a readiness shortfall in any one of these propagates.

Critical mineral extraction appears as a distinct workforce category in the employment analysis, which is evidence that the supply chain is treated as a scaling constraint. The pathway also closes off the usual escape route: it reaches net zero "without offsets from land-use measures", so biomass and CDR must come from within the energy system, with modern solid bioenergy supply at 75.7 EJ and DAC at 780 Mt CO2.

The water finding is quantified specifically for this pathway as the pathway depends more heavily on water-exposed generation, with hydro at 2 419 GW by 2050 and essentially all unabated fossil generation gone by then, so system adequacy rests more on hydrology and weather-dependent output. Physical climate impacts are still not modelled as a constraint on any lever, no adaptation requirement is quantified.

15 million new energy workers are needed worldwide by 2030, into an industry the publication says is already short of the specific trades involved.  EV and battery employment alone has to reach 10.5 million by 2030 from 2.7 million today. Given that the grid and storage build-out on which the pathway depends is already delayed partly by a shortage of qualified staff, this is a condition on the outcome rather than a cost of it.
